content: In individuals living with HIV, infection with HSV-2 is often more severe and can result in rare but serious complications, such as infections of the brain, eyes, or lungs. The 2016 WHO guidelines for the treatment of genital herpes simplex virus recommend treatment protocols that apply to all adults, adolescents aged 10–19 years, pregnant women, people living with HIV, immunocompromised individuals, and key populations such as sex workers, men who have sex with men (MSM), and transgender persons. Specific dosages for managing recurrent clinical episodes of genital HSV in people living with HIV and immunocompromised individuals are outlined in the publication. Suppressive therapy for HSV-2 should be considered in regions with high HIV prevalence. Immunocompromised patients, including those with HIV, tend to experience more frequent recurrences with more severe symptoms. Recurrent ulcers can lead to significant physical and psychological morbidity. Vulvovaginal candidiasis is a common correlate of HIV infection, often presenting as severe and recurrent. Prolonged treatment is typically required, and chronic suppressive therapy is frequently employed. For gonorrhea, the 2016 WHO guidelines for treating Neisseria gonorrhoeae infections apply to all adults and adolescents, including people living with HIV, sex workers, MSM, transgender persons, and pregnant women. Routine screening, diagnosis, and treatment of sexually transmitted infections (STIs) are essential components of comprehensive HIV prevention and care for key populations, including women living with HIV. STI management should align with existing WHO guidance and be adapted to the national context, ensuring confidentiality and informed consent. Women living with HIV are at a significantly higher risk of developing persistent HPV infections with multiple high-risk HPV types at an earlier age, leading to a more rapid progression to precancerous lesions and cervical cancer compared to women without HIV. They are 4–5 times more likely to develop cervical cancer, which is an AIDS-defining illness. The prevalence of HPV and cervical intraepithelial neoplasia (CIN) increases with greater immunosuppression. Antiretroviral therapy (ART) does not appear to improve cervical cancer outcomes. This underscores the need for specific cervical cancer vaccination, screening, and treatment protocols for women living with HIV, particularly in regions with high HIV prevalence. Screening for cervical precancer and cancer should begin as soon as a woman or girl living with HIV tests positive, regardless of age, and should be repeated 12 months after treatment for precancer or within three years after a negative screening result. Any of the three screening tests (visual inspection with acetic acid, HPV testing, or cytology) can be used, along with cryotherapy or loop electrosurgical excision procedure (LEEP) treatments. Transgender men who retain female genitalia often miss out on cervical screening and other sexual health services, increasing their risk of ovarian, uterine, and cervical diseases. Following a total hysterectomy, if there is a history of high-grade cervical dysplasia or cervical cancer, annual vaginal cuff Pap tests are recommended until three normal tests are documented, after which testing can occur every two to three years. For transgender men who have undergone oophorectomy but retain the uterus and cervix, WHO cervical screening guidelines for natal females can be followed. It is important to inform the pathologist of current or prior testosterone use, as cervical atrophy can mimic dysplasia. Cervical cancer screening for women living with HIV should be part of a standardized package of holistic, quality, confidential, non-discriminatory, and integrated HIV and sexual and reproductive health (SRH) services, including in resource-limited and rural settings, as well as in restricted environments such as prisons. Women living with HIV should be fully diagnosed, staged, and treated for cervical cancer at tertiary-level institutions with appropriate expertise. Both radiotherapy and chemotherapy are immunosuppressive, and surgery requires women to be relatively healthy to avoid complications such as postoperative sepsis, bleeding, or wound problems. Baseline CD4 counts are essential for care and should be monitored throughout treatment. If CD4 counts are low during therapy, ART may be initiated, potentially delaying treatment to allow immune system recovery. The WHO recommends the HPV vaccine for girls aged 9–13 years. Girls receiving their first dose before age 15 can follow a two-dose schedule with a six-month interval. Immunocompromised individuals, including those living with HIV, and females aged 15 years and older should receive three doses (at 0, 1–2, and 6 months) for full protection. Cervical cancer deaths are preventable, as the disease is curable if detected and treated early. Existing protocols for cervical cancer management in women living with HIV are based on experience, and ongoing studies aim to determine the best practices. The ultimate goal of these guidelines is to improve the quality of health services and SRH outcomes for women living with HIV. This requires an ethical and rights-based approach, ensuring access to high-quality, affordable health services. Investments in training healthcare providers and strengthening health systems are urgently needed to support the SRH needs and rights of women living with HIV. These efforts have far-reaching benefits for individuals, families, communities, and countries affected by HIV.
